newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey unveils revenue package but markets wary.
newsitem.headline: Turkey unveils revenue package but markets wary.

text.p: Turkish Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan on Thursday unveiled his young government's second package to raise an ambitious $10 billion for the ailing economy, but market players wanted deeds rather than words.
"We (Turkey) are needy but surrounded with wealth," Erbakan told a news conference before he announced the package. "We will utilise our potential resources and get $10 billion."

The package includes plans for selling state property, utilising unregistered precious metal stocks, imposing a new witholding tax on state securities and reducing taxes charged on domestic car sales for those who keep a 50,000 German mark ($33,000) foreign currency account.
But analysts said the market lacked confidence in the package and wanted to see implementation rather than promises.

"Both packages look fine in appearance but what is important is putting them into practice," said Hasan Soydan, securities manager at private Garanti Yatirim Bank. "The market does not look convinced," he told Reuters.
Both the stock and currency markets on Thursday closed unaffected by the revenue-raising package, analysts said, with the stock market up 0.92 percent on profit-taking.

The first package, introduced on July 31, included speedy privatisation, issuing foreign-currency denominated bonds, sale of state property, incentives and tax exemptions for Turkish workers abroad to channel their savings into the country and a six-percent charge on the financing of some imports.
But it failed to fuel optimism in the business community and markets, which saw it as unrealistic and impractical although Erbakan said on Thursday the measures had already raised $1.9 billion.

The Islamist-led government, which took power in early July in a coalition with the conservative True Path Party, aims to raise $10 billion from each of the two packages in the next three years. The government expects a budget deficit of 1,300 trillion lira ($14.4 billion) this year, up from a target of 800 trillion lira.

Erbakan said Turkey's troubled social security institutions would sell their excess property, including hotels, to finance their huge deficits, but did not give a time frame for the sell-offs that he said would raise 425 trillion lira.

The package also envisions slapping a tax on the sale of alcohol and cigarettes to get 45 trillion lira in income and introducing a 10 percent witholding tax on certain state securities, for revenue of 170 trillion lira.
Among other things, the government also wants to bring under its control unregistered precious metal stocks held by jewellers, who would have to pay a fine and thereafter be subject to related taxes.

In a bid to attract foreign currency, the plan would cut taxes on domestic car sales by 20 percent for people who deposit at least 50,000 marks in a one-year foreign currency account in Turkey. ($1=1.50 German marks) ($1=90,000 Turkish lira)
